title: Visualization with ggplot2
text:
A good visualization makes a comparison easier to see. It does not replace a definition, a data check, or a well-formed question. Before you choose a chart, identify the variables, the comparison, and the audience.
The ggplot2 package builds plots by combining layers. A typical plot specifies:

title: Visualization with ggplot2
text:
A scatter plot
A scatter plot is useful when you want to examine the relationship between two numeric variables. In the mtcars data, we can compare vehicle weight with miles per gallon.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Weight, in thousands of pounds",
    y = "Miles per gallon"
  )

Each row becomes one point. The mapping in aes() connects columns to visual properties. A trend that appears in a plot is a pattern to investigate, not automatically evidence of causation.

title: Visualization with ggplot2
text:
A bar chart
A bar chart is useful for comparing values across discrete categories. First calculate a summary at the level you want to display; then map the category and measure to the chart.

average_mpg_by_cyl <- aggregate(
  mpg ~ cyl,
  data = mtcars,
  FUN = mean
)

ggplot(average_mpg_by_cyl, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of cylinders",
    y = "Average miles per gallon"
  )

A common mistake is to use a bar chart when the x-axis is continuous or to compare totals that have different exposure levels. Always ask whether the denominator and aggregation level make the comparison fair.

title: Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Build both charts interactively
The live application below creates the scatter plot and bar chart. Try changing the x-axis, adding a color mapping, or changing the summary statistic. Notice how a small code change changes the business story the chart can tell.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]

library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

car_data <- mtcars
car_data$model <- rownames(mtcars)
car_data$transmission <- ifelse(car_data$am == 1, "Manual", "Automatic")

average_mpg_by_cyl <- aggregate(
  mpg ~ cyl,
  data = car_data,
  FUN = mean
)

scatter_plot <- ggplot(car_data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = transmission)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle weight and fuel efficiency",
    x = "Weight, in thousands of pounds",
    y = "Miles per gallon",
    color = "Transmission"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

bar_plot <- ggplot(average_mpg_by_cyl, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Average fuel efficiency by cylinder count",
    x = "Cylinders",
    y = "Average miles per gallon"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ui <- fluidPage(
  h3("Two views of the mtcars data"),
  plotOutput("scatter"),
  plotOutput("bars")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$scatter <- renderPlot(scatter_plot)
  output$bars <- renderPlot(bar_plot)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Visualization with ggplot2
text:
A visualization review checklist
Before sharing a chart, verify:

Does the chart match the type of variable and comparison?
Are the title, axes, units, and legend understandable without narration?
Does the chart use an appropriate denominator?
Are unusual values visible and explainable?
Could a different scale or aggregation change the conclusion?

An AI tool can generate attractive plotting code quickly. Your job is to check whether the chart represents the data and the decision honestly.

title: Sources Used in This Course
text: This page is a working bibliography for the course. These are the sources we used to shape the examples, explanations, technical setup, and human-in-the-loop AI workflow. The business projects are original teaching scenarios designed for this site; they are not copied case studies.

title: Sources Used in This Course
text:
R and data science foundations

R for Data Science, 2nd edition
Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund’s open textbook informed the progression from data import and transformation to visualization and communication. Its emphasis on a repeatable data-science workflow shaped the organization of the R Foundation section.


The R Project for Statistical Computing
The official R project site was used for language-level context, installation references, and the distinction between the R language and contributed packages.


R Language Definition
This official manual informed the explanations of objects, evaluation, vectors, indexing, functions, and control flow. It is a technical reference rather than a beginner tutorial.


dplyr documentation
The dplyr reference informed the descriptions of filter, select, mutate, summarise, group_by, arrange, and the behavior of grouped data.


ggplot2 documentation
The ggplot2 reference informed the visualization chapter’s explanation of data, aesthetic mappings, geometric layers, scales, and labels.

title: Sources Used in This Course
text:
Quarto and browser-based R

Quarto documentation
Quarto’s project, website, executable-document, and sidebar documentation informed the site architecture and rendering workflow.


Quarto website documentation
The website guide informed the project configuration, sidebar organization, page navigation, and static-site workflow.


Shinylive for R
The R Shinylive package documentation informed the client-side execution model and the package requirements for browser-based Shiny applications.


Shinylive Quarto extension
The extension documentation informed the live code-block syntax used throughout the course:
The live blocks use the shinylive-r code label with standalone set to true and editor/viewer components. They are complete Shiny applications so students can connect R code, data preparation, and output.

title: Sources Used in This Course
text:
AI-assisted analysis and responsible use

OpenAI Codex documentation
The Codex setup chapter uses the official OpenAI documentation for current product orientation and project-based coding workflows. Product labels, access, and permissions can change, so the official page is the source of truth for current setup details.


NIST AI Risk Management Framework
The NIST framework informed the course’s emphasis on context, evaluation, verification, validation, documentation, and human accountability when AI is used in an organizational workflow. The framework is voluntary and is not a substitute for an organization’s own policies.


NIST AI Resource Center
The AI Resource Center informed the distinction between generating an AI-assisted draft and evaluating whether an AI-enabled workflow is trustworthy for its intended use.

title: Sources Used in This Course
text:
Business-analytics inspiration
The project scenarios use familiar business-analytics patterns: regional growth reporting, customer value segmentation, store performance, operational monitoring, and stakeholder communication. These patterns were informed by the kinds of transformations emphasized in R for Data Science and by the NIST focus on defining the business context before evaluating an AI system.
The datasets in the projects are hypothetical. They are intentionally small enough for a student to inspect row by row and are not claims about any particular company, market, or benchmark.

These sources were used during design and implementation. They are not a list of fallback tutorials or a ranking of “best” resources. When a page in this course explains a package or workflow, follow the linked primary documentation for the authoritative and current version.

title: Intro to R for Business Analytics
text:
Business analysts increasingly work in partnership with AI. An assistant can draft a data import, suggest a transformation, or explain an error in seconds. The analyst still has to decide what the business question means, whether the data support the question, and whether the result is safe to share.
This course teaches the R foundation needed to direct that partnership. You will learn enough syntax and data reasoning to ask for useful code, inspect what an AI tool produced, and explain the analysis in language a stakeholder can act on.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Prompting
text: An AI coding tool can only make decisions from the context you provide. A strong prompt is a compact project brief: it identifies the data, the decision, the expected output, the tools, and the constraints.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Prompting
section: The anatomy of a strong R prompt
text:
The anatomy of a strong R prompt

1. State the business goal
Start with the decision or question, not with a function name.
Weak: “Group this data.”
Strong: “The sales director wants to compare quarterly revenue and order count across regions to decide where to focus coaching.”
The business goal gives the assistant a reason to choose an aggregation level and output format.


2. Describe the data contract
List the data frame name, column names, types, units, and a few example values. State whether each row is a transaction, customer, store-month, or another unit.
For example:

Data frame: transactions
One row: one completed order
Columns: order_id, order_date, region, customer_id, units, revenue, returned
order_date: Date
units: nonnegative integer
revenue: dollars before returns
returned: logical flag

This prevents the assistant from inventing column names or treating a transaction total as a customer-level measure.


3. Define the business terms
Words such as revenue, customer, growth, active, and best can have multiple meanings. Define them before asking for code.
Specify:

the reporting period;
whether returns, discounts, taxes, and shipping are included;
whether counts mean rows or unique identifiers;
the denominator for rates and percentages; and
how missing values should be handled.



4. Name the desired packages
If the assignment uses the tidyverse, say so. If the deliverable must use dplyr and ggplot2, say so. If the code should use only installed packages, say so.
For a Quarto or Shinylive lesson, include constraints such as:

use R;
use dplyr for wrangling and ggplot2 for plots;
write a complete self-contained example;
include comments and a plain-English explanation; and
do not use packages beyond shiny, dplyr, and ggplot2.



5. Specify the output
Describe the final artifact precisely:

one row per region;
columns for revenue, order count, and year-over-year growth;
sorted from largest to smallest growth;
a table and one chart; and
a three-sentence stakeholder interpretation.



6. Ask for assumptions and checks
Ask the assistant to list assumptions, identify possible edge cases, and suggest validation checks. This turns a one-shot answer into a reviewable draft.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Prompting
text:
Bad prompt versus good prompt

Bad prompt

Analyze my sales data in R and make a chart.

This prompt does not define the data, the period, the comparison, the package constraints, or the intended decision. A plausible response could still answer the wrong question.


Good prompt

I am preparing a regional sales review in R. The data frame is called transactions, with one row per completed order. It contains order_id, order_date, region, customer_id, units, revenue, returned, and order_year. order_date is a Date; revenue is in US dollars before returns; returned is TRUE for a fully returned order. Use dplyr and ggplot2. Keep orders from 2025 and 2026, exclude fully returned orders, calculate total net revenue and unique customer count by region and year, and calculate 2026 year-over-year revenue growth. Return a table with one row per region, sorted by growth, and a bar chart. Explain the pipeline, state assumptions, and include checks for missing regions, duplicate order IDs, and zero 2025 revenue.

The good prompt supplies a data contract, business definitions, packages, filters, metrics, output, and quality checks. Those details make the generated code easier to review.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Prompting
text:
Prompt patterns worth reusing

Ask for a plan before code

First restate the business question and propose the data transformations. Do not write code until you identify the observation unit, grouping level, measures, and assumptions.



Ask for a minimal reproducible example

If the real data are unavailable, create a small simulated data frame with the same column names and types. Make the example reproducible with a fixed random seed.



Ask for two explanations

After the code, explain each transformation twice: first in R terms and then in plain language for a nontechnical stakeholder.



Ask for a validation section

Add checks for row counts, missing values, duplicate keys, and the expected range of each calculated measure. Explain what a suspicious result would mean.



Ask for a constrained revision

Keep the existing output and variable names. Change only the calculation of net revenue and explain the change.

Narrow revision prompts reduce accidental changes elsewhere in the analysis.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Prompting
section: A prompt is a specification, not a command to trust
text:
A prompt is a specification, not a command to trust
A detailed prompt improves the first draft, but it does not guarantee correctness. Read the response as a proposed implementation of your specification. Compare every filter, join, calculation, and chart with the business definitions you supplied.
A useful habit is to keep three columns in your notes:








Prompt requirement
Code evidence
Test




Exclude returned orders
A filter on returned
Compare before and after row counts


Count unique customers
distinct customer_id
Compare with raw row count


Rank by growth
descending growth column
Inspect the first and last rows



This turns prompt quality into a practical review process.

title: Project 1: Regional Growth
text:
You are a junior analyst on a finance team. The finance manager wants a concise explanation of how regional performance changed from 2025 to 2026.
This is the first project because the core calculation is familiar but full of choices: what one row represents, how returns affect revenue, how to compare years, and what to do when the prior-year denominator is zero.

title: Project 1: Regional Growth
text:
You are a junior analyst on a finance team. The finance manager wants a concise explanation of how regional performance changed from 2025 to 2026.
This is the first project because the core calculation is familiar but full of choices: what one row represents, how returns affect revenue, how to compare years, and what to do when the prior-year denominator is zero.

title: Project 1: Regional Growth
text:
Business question

Which regions grew the most in net revenue from 2025 to 2026, and what should the finance manager know before using the ranking?

title: Project 1: Regional Growth
Project 1: Regional Growth
text:
Exact prompt to use

I am a junior business analyst working in R. Create a small reproducible hypothetical data frame named sales. Each row must represent one region-month. Include region as a character, month as an integer from 1 to 12, year as an integer, revenue as numeric dollars before returns, and returned_revenue as numeric dollars returned. Define net_revenue as revenue minus returned_revenue. Use dplyr and tidyr to keep 2025 and 2026, summarize total net revenue by region and year, reshape the result so each region has one row, and calculate year-over-year growth as (2026 net revenue minus 2025 net revenue) divided by 2025 net revenue. Return one row per region sorted by growth descending. Make the reporting period explicit, identify regions with zero or missing 2025 revenue, check for missing region values, and explain every transformation in plain English for a finance manager. Do not claim that growth proves a cause.

title: Project 1: Regional Growth
section: What to inspect in the response
text:
What to inspect in the response
Before running the code, locate:

The line that defines the row unit.
The calculation of net revenue.
The filter for comparison years.
The grouping level before summarising.
The reshaping step that puts years side by side.
The denominator used for growth.
The treatment of missing and zero prior-year revenue.
The order of the final ranking.

A frequent mistake is to calculate growth before aggregating to the region-year level. That produces a different metric: average monthly growth rather than annual regional growth.

title: Project 1: Regional Growth
Project 1: Regional Growth
Project 1: Regional Growth
text:
Extension: add decision context
Ask the AI assistant to add a second ranking based on absolute dollar change. Compare it with percentage growth. Explain why a small region can have the highest percentage growth while a large region contributes the largest dollar increase.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Getting Started
text:
An AI coding assistant is most useful when it can see the right context and when you can inspect the work it proposes. This chapter explains how to set up one assistant and establish a safe, repeatable workflow.
The examples use the ChatGPT desktop app with Codex as the primary path. Interface labels, account requirements, and availability can change, so use the current official Codex documentation and ChatGPT download page when you install the software.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Getting Started
text:
Before you install
Prepare three things:

A current R installation and an editor such as RStudio or Positron.
A folder for the course project, ideally tracked with Git.
An AI account approved for the type of data you plan to use.

Do not upload confidential customer records, credentials, or regulated information to a tool unless your organization has explicitly approved that workflow. Start with simulated or de-identified data while learning.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Getting Started
section: Option A: ChatGPT desktop app with Codex
text:
Option A: ChatGPT desktop app with Codex

Download and install

Open the official ChatGPT download page.
Choose the installer for Windows or macOS.
Run the installer and follow the operating system prompts.
Open the ChatGPT desktop app and sign in with your account.
If the app offers a product selector, choose Codex. If Codex is not available, check your account, workspace, or administrator settings before troubleshooting the project.
Start a new task and read the permissions or environment choices before accepting them.

The official OpenAI guidance describes Codex as a desktop workflow in which you sign in, choose a project, and send a first message. The app may present local, cloud, worktree, or other environment choices depending on your account and host.


Connect a local course directory

In Codex, choose the option to open a local folder or project.
Select only the course directory you want the assistant to work with.
Grant file access when prompted.
Confirm that the opened project contains the files you expect, such as _quarto.yml and the Quarto documents.
Ask the assistant to inspect the project before asking it to edit anything.
Keep your original files under version control so changes can be reviewed or reverted safely.

A useful first message is:

Inspect this Quarto project and summarize its current architecture. Do not modify files. Identify the site configuration, source pages, extensions, and any generated output directories.



Learn the interface
Most coding-agent interfaces have some version of these areas:

A conversation or task panel for instructions and explanations.
A file or project context area showing what the assistant can access.
A terminal or command area for commands such as quarto render.
A change or diff view where you can review proposed edits.
An approval or permission control for commands, file access, and external connections.

Treat the diff as part of the analytical workflow. Read what changed, ask why it changed, and run the smallest relevant test before accepting a large revision.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Getting Started
section: Option B: GitHub Copilot in VS Code
text:
Option B: GitHub Copilot in VS Code

Install Visual Studio Code.
Open Extensions and search for GitHub Copilot.
Install the official GitHub Copilot extension.
Sign in with the GitHub account or organization that provides Copilot access.
Open the course folder in VS Code.
Create or open an R script or Quarto document.
Use Copilot Chat to describe the business question and ask for an explanation before requesting code.
Review suggested edits and run the code in RStudio, Quarto, or the Shinylive playground.

Copilot is integrated into the editor; Codex can work across a project with a broader task-oriented workflow. The review principles are the same: provide context, inspect changes, run tests, and protect sensitive data.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Getting Started
section: Option C: Claude or Claude Code
text:
Option C: Claude or Claude Code
You can use the same workflow with Claude or Claude Code documentation:

Create or sign in to an approved account.
Install the desktop or command-line tool appropriate for your environment.
Open the course folder only after checking the tool’s local-file permissions.
Provide the project context and business question.
Ask for a plan and assumptions before asking for edits.
Paste generated code into your R or Quarto workflow, then test it independently.

The tool may have different file, terminal, and approval controls. Learn those controls before using it with a real project.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Getting Started
text:
A safe first-session checklist
Before allowing an assistant to make changes, confirm:

I know which folder it can read and write.
I know whether it is operating locally or in a cloud environment.
I have a recoverable copy or Git commit.
I have removed secrets and confidential records.
I know how to inspect a diff.
I have a small test command ready, such as quarto render.
I can explain the business definition the code is supposed to implement.

Setup is successful when the assistant can see the appropriate project context and you can independently verify every material change.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Debugging
text:
Debugging is not a separate activity from analysis. It is the process of comparing what the code did with what you intended, then narrowing the difference until you can make a justified change.
An AI assistant can accelerate debugging, but only if you give it precise evidence and keep control of the test.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Debugging
text:
Read the console in layers

Output
Printed output is the value an expression returned. Inspect whether it has the expected number of rows, columns, groups, units, and range.
A table with zero rows is output, not an error. It may mean a filter excluded everything.


Warnings
A warning means R completed an operation but wants you to review something. Common causes include missing values, failed type conversions, or values that could not be summarized.
Do not hide warnings just to make a report look clean. Decide whether the warning indicates a data-quality problem, an expected edge case, or a mistake.


Errors
An error means the requested operation did not complete. Read the final message and the function named near the top of the message. The error location is evidence about what R expected and what it received.


Messages
Messages are informational notices, such as package startup notes. They are not automatically failures.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Debugging
text:
A repeatable debugging loop

Step 1: Reproduce the smallest failure
Run the smallest section of code that still produces the problem. If a long pipeline fails, execute the import, then the first transformation, then the next. This tells you which step changes the data into an unexpected shape.


Step 2: Capture the evidence
Copy:

the exact error or warning;
the smallest code that reproduces it;
the output of names(data), dim(data), and str(data);
the expected behavior; and
any relevant package versions or file details.

Do not send only “it does not work.” The assistant needs the mismatch, not just the conclusion.


Step 3: Ask for explanation before a rewrite
Use a prompt that asks the AI to diagnose the cause, explain the relevant R concept, and propose the smallest targeted fix. Ask it not to rewrite unrelated code.


Step 4: Apply one change
Make one change in your own script. If you change five things at once, you will not know which change solved the problem or created a new one.


Step 5: Test the fix
Run the smallest reproducing example again. Then run the full analysis and compare the output with the original business requirement.


Step 6: Record the lesson
Write down what failed, why it failed, what fixed it, and how you verified the fix. A debugging note becomes a reusable review rule.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Debugging
text:
Common error patterns







Message or symptom
What to investigate




object ‘x’ not found
Misspelled name, wrong execution order, or object created in a different scope


could not find function
Package is missing, not loaded, or the function name is wrong


undefined columns selected
Column name does not match the data


non-numeric argument to binary operator
Text, factors, or missing values are being used in arithmetic


replacement has length zero
The object being assigned has no values or the index is empty


unexpected results with no error
Wrong filter, join, grouping level, sign, unit, or denominator



The final row is particularly important in business analytics. Correct syntax can still produce an incorrect business result.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Debugging
text:
A debugging prompt template

I am working in R. Here is the smallest code that reproduces the issue: [paste code]. Here is the exact console output: [paste the complete message]. The data have these columns and types: [paste names and structure]. I expected: [describe expected behavior]. Please explain the likely cause in plain English, identify the specific line involved, suggest the smallest fix, and give me one test that will verify the fix. Do not rewrite unrelated parts of the code.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Debugging
text:
Reverse-engineer the proposed fix
When the AI suggests a change, ask:

What assumption about the data does this fix rely on?
Does it change the result or only suppress the error?
Will it work for missing values, empty groups, and new categories?
Does it preserve the business definition?
What test would fail if the fix were wrong?

For example, if a tool suggests converting a character column to numeric, first inspect the values. Currency symbols, commas, text such as “unknown,” and empty strings may require different handling.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Project Map
text:
These projects practice the full workflow: define a business question, specify a data contract, ask an AI tool for a reproducible R solution, and review the result against the request.
Each project is a standalone mini-case. Open the project page, copy its exact prompt into ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or another approved assistant, and then evaluate the returned code in your own environment.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Project Map
text:
A progression in analytical complexity

Project 1: Regional Growth
Begin with grouped summaries and a year-over-year metric. This project emphasizes observation units, time periods, denominators, and edge cases such as zero prior-year revenue.


Project 2: Customer Value
Move from order-level data to customer-level features and business-defined segments. This project emphasizes unique identifiers, reproducible date windows, thresholds, and missing data.


Project 3: Store Operations
Combine financial, operational, and quality measures in a stakeholder-facing application. This project emphasizes validation checks, descriptive versus causal claims, and the limits of a single ranking.

title: AI Coding Workflow: Project Map
Project 2: Customer Value
text:
You are an analyst supporting a subscription business. The marketing team wants a simple, transparent customer-value segmentation that can be used to prioritize outreach.
This project increases complexity by moving from order-level records to customer-level features. The central review question is whether the code counts and summarizes at the correct level.

title: Project 2: Customer Value
text:
You are an analyst supporting a subscription business. The marketing team wants a simple, transparent customer-value segmentation that can be used to prioritize outreach.
This project increases complexity by moving from order-level records to customer-level features. The central review question is whether the code counts and summarizes at the correct level.

title: Project 2: Customer Value
text:
Business question

Which customers are Low, Core, or High value based on completed spending in the last twelve months, and how large is each segment?

title: Project 2: Customer Value
text:
Data contract
Ask the AI assistant to create a reproducible hypothetical data frame called orders with:

customer_id: character identifier;
order_date: Date;
order_value: numeric dollars; and
status: character order status.

Each row represents one order. The analysis should use completed orders only and should define a fixed analysis date so that the results can be reproduced.
Use these segment rules:

Low: total completed spend below 500;
Core: total completed spend from 500 through 1,999.99; and
High: total completed spend of 2,000 or more.

title: Project 2: Customer Value
text:
Exact prompt to use

Write a reproducible R analysis using dplyr for a hypothetical data frame named orders. Each row represents one order. The columns are customer_id as character, order_date as Date, order_value as numeric dollars, and status as character. Create a fixed analysis_date in the example and keep only completed orders in the twelve months ending on that date. Exclude or clearly report missing customer IDs and missing order values. Summarize total completed spend, order count, and average order value for each unique customer_id. Classify customers as Low when total spend is below 500, Core when total spend is from 500 through 1,999.99, and High when total spend is 2,000 or more. Return both a customer-level table and a segment summary with customer count, total spend, and average customer spend. Include checks for duplicate order IDs, unexpected status values, missing dates, and whether the segment thresholds cover every customer. Explain the transformations in plain English for a marketing manager.

title: Project 2: Customer Value
section: What to inspect in the response
text:
What to inspect in the response
Focus on the difference between an order and a customer:

Is the segment assigned after grouping by customer_id?
Is order count counted before or after customer aggregation?
Are incomplete, cancelled, or returned orders treated consistently?
Is the twelve-month period inclusive and reproducible?
Is average order value different from average customer spend?
Are customers with missing IDs excluded from the segment table?
Are the threshold boundaries implemented exactly?

An AI tool may use n() when the requirement is a unique customer count. That is correct in the customer-level table only if one row has already been created per customer.

title: Project 2: Customer Value
Project 2: Customer Value
Project 2: Customer Value
section: Extension: compare threshold and quantile approaches
text:
Extension: compare threshold and quantile approaches
Ask the AI assistant to create a second version using quantiles rather than fixed dollar thresholds. Compare the interpretability, stability, and business usefulness of the two approaches. Explain which method you would recommend and why.

title: Project 3: Store Operations
text:
You are supporting a retail operations director who wants to identify stores that combine strong sales with manageable checkout times. The request sounds like a ranking problem, but it actually combines data quality, financial measures, operational measures, and communication risk.
This project is intentionally multi-faceted. A polished table is not enough; the analysis must show what was included, how the metrics were defined, and what the evidence cannot prove.

title: Project 3: Store Operations
text:
You are supporting a retail operations director who wants to identify stores that combine strong sales with manageable checkout times. The request sounds like a ranking problem, but it actually combines data quality, financial measures, operational measures, and communication risk.
This project is intentionally multi-faceted. A polished table is not enough; the analysis must show what was included, how the metrics were defined, and what the evidence cannot prove.

title: Project 3: Store Operations
text:
Business question

Which stores are performing strongly, which stores may need an operational review, and what evidence supports those observations?

title: Project 3: Store Operations
Project 3: Store Operations
text:
Exact prompt to use

Build a self-contained R/Shiny example using shiny and dplyr for a hypothetical data frame named transactions. Each row represents one transaction. Columns are store_id as character, transaction_id as character, transaction_date as Date, sales as numeric dollars, units as integer, and checkout_minutes as numeric. Create a reproducible example with a fixed seed. Before summarising, report rows missing store_id or transaction_id, duplicate transaction IDs, negative sales, and missing operational measures. Exclude rows missing store_id or transaction_id, but do not silently discard them. Calculate one row per store with unique transaction count, total sales, total units, average basket value, average units per transaction, and median checkout time. Add an operational_watch flag when median checkout time is above 8 minutes. Sort the summary by total sales descending. Display the quality checks, the store summary, and a cautious plain-English interpretation. Explain that the results are descriptive and do not prove that checkout time causes sales performance. Use only shiny and dplyr.

title: Project 3: Store Operations
section: What to inspect in the response
text:
What to inspect in the response
This project has several opportunities for an AI-generated script to look reasonable while being wrong:

Does the code count unique transactions or raw rows?
Are invalid rows reported before they are removed?
Does a negative sale get hidden in a total?
Is average basket value total sales divided by transaction count?
Is average units per transaction calculated at the store level?
Is median used intentionally for checkout time?
Does the operational flag apply to the same store-level summary?
Does the narrative overstate correlation as causation?

The phrase “best store” is deliberately avoided. A store can lead in sales while having slow checkout, or have fast checkout while serving a smaller customer base.

title: Project 3: Store Operations
text:
Testing protocol
Use a small manual test with a store that has two transactions: 100 dollars and 50 dollars, with one unit and two units. Its total sales should be 150, transaction count should be 2, average basket value should be 75, and average units per transaction should be 1.5.
Then test the quality checks by adding:

a missing store identifier;
a duplicate transaction ID;
a negative sales value; and
a missing checkout time.

Confirm that the code reports each issue and that the summary’s inclusion rules are visible.

title: Project 3: Store Operations
Project 3: Store Operations
text:
Extension: build a decision matrix
Ask the AI assistant to add a four-quadrant classification using sales rank and checkout-time rank:

strong sales and manageable checkout;
strong sales and operational watch;
lower sales and manageable checkout; and
lower sales and operational watch.

Require the assistant to explain the cutoffs, identify their arbitrariness, and preserve the original measures beside the classification. This is a more decision-oriented output, but it also introduces more assumptions for you to audit.

title: Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
Business data rarely arrives in the exact shape needed for a decision. Data wrangling is the process of selecting relevant observations, creating useful measures, grouping records, and producing a summary that answers a question.
The dplyr package organizes these tasks into a small set of readable verbs. A pipeline expresses the transformation as a sequence from top to bottom.

title: Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
The pipe
The base R pipe, written as |>, passes the result of the expression on its left into the function on its right:

mtcars |>
  head()

Many R courses also use the pipe from magrittr, written as %>%. Both styles support the same general idea. The base pipe is part of modern R and avoids requiring a separate package for the pipe itself.

title: Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
The core dplyr verbs

filter(): choose rows
Use filter() to keep observations that satisfy a condition. In a business dataset, this might mean a date range, region, customer segment, or product category.

mtcars |>
  dplyr::filter(cyl >= 6)



select(): choose columns
Use select() to keep only the variables needed for the next step or the final report.

mtcars |>
  dplyr::select(mpg, cyl, hp, wt)



mutate(): create variables
Use mutate() to add or modify columns. Every derived measure should have a clear definition and compatible units.

mtcars |>
  dplyr::mutate(power_to_weight = hp / wt)



summarise(): reduce rows to metrics
Use summarise() to calculate a smaller set of values, often after grouping. Common summary functions include mean(), sum(), median(), min(), max(), and n().


group_by(): define the comparison
group_by() tells dplyr to calculate summaries separately for each group. A summary without grouping answers a different question from a summary by region, segment, or month.


arrange(): sort the result
Use arrange() to order rows. Add desc() inside arrange() when the largest values should appear first.

title: Data Wrangling with dplyr
Data Wrangling with dplyr
section: Read the pipeline as a business analyst
text:
Read the pipeline as a business analyst
A pipeline is not automatically correct because it is readable. Ask:

Does the filter include the population the stakeholder intended?
Are the selected columns sufficient to audit the calculation?
Are the units compatible in every mutate() expression?
Is the grouping level appropriate for the decision?
Does the summary hide important variation?
Is the sort order emphasizing the right outcome?

These questions are equally important when the pipeline was written by you or generated by an AI assistant.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
R is both a programming language and an environment for working with data. A business analyst uses R to represent a question, transform observations, calculate measures, visualize patterns, and create a record of the work.
This chapter builds the vocabulary needed to read and direct R code generated by an AI assistant.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
1. R as a calculator
R can evaluate arithmetic expressions:

revenue <- 185000
cost <- 112000
profit <- revenue - cost
margin <- profit / revenue

The assignment operator <- stores a result under a name. The expression on the right is evaluated first. Use descriptive names that communicate the business meaning of an object.

Operators
Common operators include:



Operator
Meaning
Example




+, -, *, /
Arithmetic
revenue - cost


^
Exponent
growth_rate ^ 2


==
Equal to
region == “North”


!=
Not equal to
status != “Cancelled”


>, <, >=, <=
Comparison
revenue >= 10000


&, |
And, or for vectors
active & revenue > 0


!
Not
!returned



The single equals sign is used inside function arguments or assignments in other languages, while R commonly uses <- for assignment and == for comparison.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
2. Core data types
R uses different data types to represent different kinds of information:








Type
Example
Business use




Numeric
185000, 0.12
Revenue, quantity, margin, rate


Character
“North”, “Enterprise”
Region, segment, product label


Logical
TRUE, FALSE
Flags such as active or approved


Integer
1L, 12L
Counts and positions


Date
as.Date(“2026-01-15”)
Transaction dates and reporting periods



Inspect an object with class(), typeof(), and str():

amount <- 185000
region <- "North"
approved <- TRUE
report_date <- as.Date("2026-01-15")

class(amount)
typeof(region)
str(list(amount = amount, region = region, approved = approved, report_date = report_date))

A type mismatch is a common source of errors. A number stored as character text cannot be reliably added to another number until it is cleaned and converted. A date stored as text may sort alphabetically rather than chronologically.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
3. Vectors
A vector is a sequence of values. Most columns in a business dataset are vectors, with one value for each observation.

regions <- c("North", "South", "West")
sales <- c(42000, 38500, 51750)
is_target_met <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

length(regions)
sales * 1.05
sales > 40000

R performs element-by-element operations on vectors. Be careful when vectors have different lengths: R may recycle the shorter vector, which can be useful but can also hide a mistake.
Missing values are represented by NA. Test for them with is.na(); do not compare with == NA.

scores <- c(91, 87, NA, 94)

is.na(scores)
mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

The business decision about missing data belongs in the analysis plan. Removing missing values can change the population being described.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
4. Indexing and subsetting
Use square brackets to select positions or conditions:

sales[1]
sales[1:2]
sales[sales > 40000]
regions[sales > 40000]

The expression sales > 40000 produces a logical vector. Using that vector inside brackets keeps only the corresponding values. This pattern is the foundation for filtering rows in more advanced tools.
Use the dollar sign to select a named column from a data frame:

regional_sales <- data.frame(
  region = regions,
  sales = sales,
  target_met = is_target_met
)

regional_sales$region
regional_sales[regional_sales$sales > 40000, ]

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
5. Data frames and tibbles
A data frame combines equal-length vectors into rows and columns. Each row can represent a transaction, customer, store, or month. Each column represents a variable or measure.

head(regional_sales)
nrow(regional_sales)
ncol(regional_sales)
names(regional_sales)
summary(regional_sales)

A tibble is a modern data-frame format used throughout the tidyverse. It prints compactly and makes column behavior easier to inspect. The two structures represent rectangular data; the difference is mostly in printing and modern defaults.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
6. Functions
A function packages a reusable operation. Functions take arguments and return a result:

mean(sales)
round(mean(sales), digits = 0)
sort(sales, decreasing = TRUE)

You can write your own function when a calculation will be repeated:

margin_rate <- function(revenue, cost) {
  (revenue - cost) / revenue
}

margin_rate(185000, 112000)

A good business function has clear inputs, a clear output, and a definition that a stakeholder can understand.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
8. Repetition and iteration
Many business transformations can be expressed with vectorized operations and dplyr. Base R also provides loops and apply functions for repeated work.

monthly_sales <- c(42000, 38500, 51750)

for (month_sales in monthly_sales) {
  print(month_sales * 1.05)
}

Loops are useful, but they are not automatically better. Ask an AI assistant to explain whether a vectorized or grouped solution is clearer before accepting a complex loop.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
9. Packages, scripts, and projects
R’s core installation is extended by packages. A package may provide functions, datasets, documentation, and dependencies.

install.packages() downloads a package once;
library() makes an installed package available in a session;
package documentation describes intended behavior; and
a project folder keeps scripts, data, and rendered outputs organized.

A reproducible analysis records the packages and versions it relies on. When an AI-generated script begins with several library() calls, treat them as part of the data contract, not as decoration.

title: R Basics: A Complete Foundation
text:
10. Practice in a live application
The application below creates objects of several basic types and shows how vectors become a data frame. Run it, then edit the values. Try adding a region, changing a logical flag, or calculating a new margin column.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]

library(shiny)

regions <- c("North", "South", "West")
sales <- c(42000, 38500, 51750)
is_target_met <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

regional_sales <- data.frame(
  region = regions,
  sales = sales,
  target_met = is_target_met
)

regional_sales$margin <- c(0.31, 0.27, 0.34)

ui <- fluidPage(
  h3("R objects, types, vectors, and data frames"),
  p("The table combines vectors into a small business dataset."),
  h4("Object inspection"),
  verbatimTextOutput("types"),
  h4("Regional sales data"),
  tableOutput("sales_table")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$types <- renderPrint({
    list(
      regions_class = class(regions),
      sales_class = class(sales),
      target_flag_class = class(is_target_met),
      table_dimensions = c(nrow(regional_sales), ncol(regional_sales)),
      column_names = names(regional_sales)
    )
  })

  output$sales_table <- renderTable({
    regional_sales
  }, digits = 2)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
